title: Summer Avot
hookLine: a chapter of Pirkei Avot each summer Shabbat afternoon
tomorrow: why would anyone skip haircuts for three weeks?

lines: A BORROWED LINE BEFORE AND AFTER.
cards: Long summer afternoons have a way of dissolving: a nap, a screen, and suddenly the light is gone. Some Jews give one of those hours, on Shabbat, to a short book of sayings: Pirkei Avot, a chapter a week.
Open a siddur to it and something looks odd. Before each chapter sits a line that isn't from Avot. After it, another line from somewhere else entirely.
Why would every chapter start with a borrowed line?

teach.h: BEFORE: A SHARE FOR ALL ISRAEL.
teach.b: The line before comes from another part of the Mishnah, tractate Sanhedrin: all Israel have a share in the world to come.

teach.h: AFTER: MUCH TORAH, AS A GIFT.
teach.b: The line after comes from tractate Makkot: Rabbi Chananya ben Akashya says the Holy One wanted to give Israel merit, and so gave them much Torah and many commandments.
So every chapter of hard, practical advice sits between two promises: you belong, and all of this is a gift. That's the puzzle solved. And the sayings inside can sting.

Avot opens with a chain, Moses received Torah at Sinai and handed it on, to say these short lines are Torah too, passed hand to hand. Then: be deliberate in judgment. Hillel: if I am not for myself, who will be for me?
Rabbi Tarfon: it is not your duty to finish the work, but neither are you free to stop. Read cold, that's a lot of pressure for a lazy afternoon.
Read inside the frame, it changes: you already have a place, and the work is handed to you, not dumped on you.
The custom is a chapter each Shabbat afternoon through the summer months, and some go around the cycle more than once. One chapter takes a few minutes. Slow enough to remember one saying by Sunday.

how: Some Jewish communities read a chapter of Pirkei Avot on Shabbat afternoons in the summer, each chapter introduced by Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1 and closed with the saying of Rabbi Chananya ben Akashya.

s: Pirkei Avot is a book of laws
it sits in the Mishnah, but it's sayings about how to live.
in the siddur, each chapter of Avot is framed by lines from other tractates
Sanhedrin before: a share in the world to come. Makkot after: much Torah, as a gift.
Avot opens by naming its author
it opens with a chain: Moses received Torah at Sinai and handed it on.

games.q: summer job, your little sister, your grandpa's garden: too much to do, and Sunday is already here. which Avot saying fits?
o: Rabbi Tarfon: not yours to finish, not free to stop.
be deliberate in judgment: decide nothing until you're sure.
if I am not for myself: drop the rest and rest.
games.why: Tarfon's line is made for this: do your part of the work without carrying the whole of it. Hillel's line goes on: if I am only for myself, what am I?

practice: Choose one saying from today, maybe Rabbi Tarfon's: not yours to finish, not free to stop. Stand, if you can, and walk slowly for about a minute, saying it silently in time with your steps.
When you sit back down, notice which half of the line stayed with you.

sources.ref: Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1 (all Israel have a share in the world to come), read before each chapter
